title: The Differential Role of Executive Functions in Reading Fluency in Children With Reading Difficulties, Children With Autism and Typically Developing Children.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Reading fluency depends in part on executive functions (EF). Dysfluent reading and reduced EF occur in both autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and reading disability (RD), but whether the EF-reading fluency associations established in RD also characterize ASD is unclear. We tested whether diagnostic group moderates these associations.
METHODS: Two hundred twenty-three English-speaking children aged 8-12 years with ASD (n = 35), RD (n = 99), and typical development (TD; n = 89) completed measures of single-word, pseudoword, and contextual reading fluency, working memory (Digit Span), and processing speed (Coding, Symbol Search). Welch's ANOVAs compared groups; linear models with Group×EF interactions and simple slopes tested moderation, with age covaried in sensitivity models.
RESULTS: Both clinical groups showed lower reading fluency and EF than TD. Coding predicted word and pseudoword fluency most strongly in ASD (β = 0.40 and 0.43) and less strongly in TD, but not in RD. Digit span predicted word fluency in ASD, and pseudoword fluency in ASD and RD. For contextual fluency, a significant Group × Symbol Search interaction (p = .003) indicated that symbol search predicted performance in ASD (β = 0.52) and TD (β = 0.29) but not RD. Results were unchanged with age covaried.
CONCLUSION: EF-reading fluency associations were strongest and most widespread in ASD, whereas in RD executive measures predicted decoding-level but not contextual fluency. Comparable dysfluency thus rests on distinct executive profiles, supporting the inclusion of EF measures in reading assessment for children with autism and cautioning against transferring RD-derived interventions without adaptation.
